summary:
Çorum province stands under the national framework applicable across Türkiye, and that framework presents a structured and documented danger to trans visitors. The sources assembled for this province record no Çorum-specific enforcement actions or incidents; the findings below are national, and they are what a visitor to Çorum would be subject to.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft of Türkiye's 11th Judicial Package would amend penal-code article 225 to punish conduct "contrary to biological sex" with up to three years in prison, and would allow charges against anyone taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony, carrying up to four years. Under civil-code article 40 the same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25 and impose a permanent-infertility mandate, with providers facing fines and up to seven years and patients up to three years. Fifteen LGBTI+ organisations and the Turkish Medical Association objected, and Human Rights Watch called for withdrawal. Whether the package has been enacted remains unresolved in the sources.

Criminalisation by statute had not been enacted when Human Rights Watch reported, but the reform sits within a broader authoritarian drift in which the government has repeatedly framed LGBTI+ life as a threat to the family and to public morals. Kaos GL's LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025, published 24 February 2026, finds that hostility hardened into explicit state policy over the year under "Year of the Family" instructions.

The same report documents 313 right-to-liberty violations across 2025, about two and a half times the previous year and mostly detentions, alongside 89 torture and ill-treatment violations, up from 51, and six right-to-life violations of which three were hate-motivated killings, with transgender people the group most affected. Türkiye keeps no official hate-crime statistics, so these figures rest on media monitoring rather than state records, which means the true scale is not established.

Identity checks on the street are a direct visitor risk. In August 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women while they were walking, shopping or sitting in cafés in Beyoğlu, held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station and released them after "General Information Gathering" background checks. Legal experts quoted by bianet argue those checks breach Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Nothing was fined; names and details were recorded, and officers applied a regime that had not been enacted. Foreigners must separately carry original photo ID at transit checkpoints in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and warnings of detention for non-compliance.

Policing asymmetry is documented at the level of individual cases. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy by a 17-year-old; the attacker was released while the victim herself was referred for arrest, which activists describe as evidence of a state hate policy. On 1 December 2025 the transgender prisoner Poyraz was found dead in his cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers state that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, medical staff arrived after prolonged delay, prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison only two days later, and witness statements were not taken; an opposition MP raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025.

Trans visitors who are detained are held in facilities organised by registered sex rather than gender identity. Turkish prisons subject LGBTI+ detainees to arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation and restricted healthcare; some prisoners refuse hospital transfers for fear of other male inmates. No policy or staff training exists to identify LGBTI+ needs, complaints mechanisms are ineffective and can provoke further violence, and transfers are frequent.

Protection machinery is thin. Türkiye has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity, and no direct discrimination protection for gender identity. The European Commission's 2025 report found legal protection insufficient and out of line with the EU acquis, while noting official permissions granted to demonstrations promoting exclusion. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through the year, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia. If medication is needed during a stay, hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system, so trans visitors must obtain and pay for it privately.
tangentialFactors:
The 2025 pattern is national rather than local: Kaos GL's report is compiled at country level and contains no province-specific breakdown, so Çorum cannot be distinguished from Istanbul or Ankara on any of the recorded indicators. A visitor should read the country-wide figures as the baseline exposure anywhere in Türkiye, including Çorum.

The state's own evidentiary gap shapes how the risk can be assessed. Because no official hate-crime statistics are kept, documentation depends on media coverage and NGO monitoring, which systematically undercounts rather than overcounts. Independent estimates therefore sit above anything the authorities publish.

Legislative drift is the main unsettled variable. The draft 11th Judicial Package would move conduct that is currently unpunished into the penal code and would tighten gender-affirming care rules to 25 years plus permanent infertility; whether that package has passed is unresolved in the sources, so a visitor may arrive before or after a material change in the law.

Comparison with the European Union accession framework is documented rather than implied: the European Commission's 2025 assessment holds Türkiye's anti-discrimination protection out of line with the EU acquis, while the same period saw official permissions granted to demonstrations promoting exclusion. The gap between accession standards and domestic practice has widened rather than narrowed.

Visibility carries its own exposure. Attendance at the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week coincided with violations of international human-rights law that monitoring has tracked continuously since 2015, and with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric. Public assembly is a documented flashpoint rather than a protected routine.
localsOnly:
Resident trans people in Türkiye face the same draft provisions reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025: penal-code article 225 would criminalise conduct "contrary to biological sex" with up to three years, charges would extend to participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies at up to four years, and civil-code article 40 would raise the age for gender-affirming care to 25 with a permanent-infertility mandate, providers facing fines and up to seven years and patients up to three years. Fifteen LGBTI+ organisations and the Turkish Medical Association objected and Human Rights Watch sought withdrawal.

Detention statistics for residents are dominated by liberty violations: 313 in 2025, roughly two and a half times the 2024 figure and mostly detentions, of which the earlier national reporting counted 256 taken on the record and 43 off it. A further 89 torture and ill-treatment violations were recorded against 51 the previous year, and six right-to-life violations included three hate-motivated killings, with transgender people most affected.

Detention conditions for residents are governed by registered sex rather than gender identity. LGBTI+ detainees are subjected to body and strip searches, de facto isolation and restricted healthcare, complaints can provoke further violence, and transfers are frequent with no staff training on LGBTI+ needs. The death of the transgender prisoner Poyraz at Sincan Women's Prison on 1 December 2025 drew demands from rights groups for an independent investigation and changes to detention practice; an opposition MP raised it in parliament on 12 December 2025.

Residents have no statutory discrimination complaint to file on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, since no comprehensive prohibition exists and gender identity is not directly protected. Hate-crime data is not compiled by the state, so recorded cases depend on media monitoring. Gender-affirming medication is not covered by the public healthcare system and is paid for privately.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 11th Judicial Package described by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025 has since been enacted is unresolved in the sources; the inventory records it as a leaked draft before the government with objections pending.

No source in the inventory records any enforcement action, detention, prosecution, incident or facility condition specific to Çorum. The province profile rests entirely on national material, and the absence of Çorum-level reporting should not be read as an absence of risk.

The distinction between detentions taken on the record and those taken off it (256 and 43 in the national figures) comes from earlier national reporting rather than the Kaos GL report cited here, and is included as context for the 313 total.

The inventory does not establish whether the 2025 violations recorded by Kaos GL occurred in Çorum, and it does not resolve how many of the six right-to-life violations involved visitors rather than residents. Both remain not sourced.
